arabic_learner_risk_hypotheses.statement: Some learners may merge English /p/ and /b/ in perception or production.
Some learners may merge English /v/ and /f/ in perception or production.
English /θ/ and /ð/ may be replaced by different stops or fricatives; patterns vary by Arabic dialect.
Some learners may add /g/ after /ŋ/ or replace it in unfamiliar word positions.
Contrasts such as /iː/-/ɪ/ and /uː/-/ʊ/ may need explicit perception and meaning-based practice.
English /æ/, /e/, /ʌ/, and related vowels may be mapped onto a smaller learner-specific set.
Some learners may insert a vowel into unfamiliar initial or final consonant clusters.
Final consonants or clusters may be reduced when several articulatory demands occur together.
Plural, third-person, possessive, and past endings may be omitted or given an extra syllable.
Stress may follow spelling or a familiar Arabic pattern rather than the English lexical pattern.
Function words may receive equal prominence, limiting English focus and rhythm cues.
English spelling may encourage a stable letter-to-sound guess where pronunciation is irregular.

rules: Assess intelligibility inside fresh communicative performance; isolated imitation may diagnose but cannot prove mastery.
Score listener effort, preservation of key meaning, segmental clarity, stress and prominence, chunking, and repair at the level boundary.
Keep receptive sound discrimination separate from productive pronunciation control.
Permit the clarification and repair support named by the learner's level; do not silently score an A1 speaker as C2.
Never deduct for a retained accent when meaning, intelligibility, effectiveness, and situational appropriateness are preserved.

limitations: CEFR evidence validates level boundaries, not this English-specific teaching order.
Arabic-learner risks are dialect-sensitive hypotheses until specialist review and learner observation.
Exact phoneme targets and task locations are selected during level reconciliation from communication need and observed breakdowns.
